ui.honestHeading: What is real and what is drawn
ui.honest: The close-up shows every atom the crystal structure 1MAB records for the head of rat liver ATP synthase, built into the full ring of six from the file's own symmetry. The machine view is a drawing: the membrane, the ring, the stalks and the proton door are simple shapes, and the motion is slowed down a lot. The head is drawn at its measured width. The counts are real: 8 c-subunits in the ring, 8 protons and 3 ATP per turn, as measured for cow mitochondria and expected for other animals with backbones.
ui.alt: An illustrative 3D drawing of ATP synthase sitting in the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Below the membrane is the intermembrane space; above it is the matrix. In the membrane, a ring of 8 teal c-subunits spins like a turnstile. Glowing yellow protons come up from below, enter through a red proton door beside the ring, ride around on the ring, and leave into the matrix above. A blue central stalk spins with the ring and turns inside the big head above the membrane, a ring of three pink alpha and three gold beta parts, which a grey side stalk holds still. Each time the stalk turns a third of the way, one beta part pushes out a new ATP molecule. Counters show 8 protons going in for every 3 ATP made. The real atoms view shows the head from the crystal structure 1MAB as thousands of coloured spheres, with ATP and ADP held between the alpha and beta parts.

machine.h: A spinning machine that makes ATP
machine.t: Protons pile up below the membrane. The only way back up is through this machine, and as they flow through, they spin the ring and the stalk. The turning stalk squeezes the head, which makes ATP.

closeup.t: Three alpha and three beta parts form a ring around the gamma stalk. ATP and ADP sit where alpha meets beta. Each coloured sphere is one atom from the crystal structure.

facts.t: ATP synthase sits in the inner membrane of mitochondria. It works like a tiny generator: hydrogen ions (protons) flowing through it turn part of it, and the turning adds a phosphate to ADP to make ATP.
The protons get there because the cell pumps them from the matrix into the intermembrane space. ATP synthase is their only way back through the membrane.

It is two motors in one: Fo in the membrane, turned by protons, and F1 in the head, where ATP is made. The head sticks out into the matrix and is joined to the membrane part by a central stalk and a side stalk.
Each c-subunit in the ring carries a glutamate near the middle of the membrane. It picks up a proton, rides around, and lets it go, one proton per c-subunit per turn.
Each full turn makes 3 ATP. In cow mitochondria the ring has 8 c-subunits, so one turn moves 8 protons: about 2.7 protons per ATP. Animals with backbones probably all have rings of 8.
Other living things build bigger rings: 10 to 15 c-subunits in fungi, bacteria and plant chloroplasts.
In a living cell the ring and stalk spin about 100 times a second.
This way of making ATP, called chemiosmosis, makes 90 percent of the ATP a cell gets from breaking down glucose with oxygen.

The real atoms are the F1 head of rat liver ATP synthase, PDB 1MAB, solved by X-ray at 2.8 angstroms. Measured from the file, the ring of six is 12.1 nm across and 10.6 nm tall. Only 124 of gamma's 270 amino acids show up in the crystal.
